items.author: DecryptMedia
items.context: @DecryptMedia (229.173 seguidores), en inglés: "Coldcard Bitcoin Exploit, Revisited: How a Hidden Flaw Survived Years of Audits" (enlace a decrypt.co). Según el artículo: Coinkite publicó el postmortem; de marzo 2021 a julio 2026 el firmware generó semillas con un PRNG de software (Yasmarang) en vez del RNG de hardware, con ~40-72 bits de entropía efectiva en vez de 128; al menos 15 revisiones (2 auditorías pagadas) no lo detectaron; ~300 tickets de pérdida en 242 cuentas; la actualización no repara semillas ya creadas. Publicado hace ~10 min, sin respuestas aún. Ángulo: autocustodia y entropía verificable.
items.suggested_text:
The detail that matters most here is that the seeds looked fine. From 2021 to July 2026 the firmware used a software PRNG instead of the hardware RNG, leaving roughly 40 to 72 bits of effective randomness instead of 128, and at least 15 reviews, including two paid audits, missed it because each one checked that the RNG code existed, not that seed generation actually reached it.

That's the uncomfortable lesson for self-custody: when your seed is created inside a closed device, you inherit every assumption in its build pipeline. A firmware update closes the bug, but it can't repair seeds already generated. Those funds stay exposed until they're moved to a new seed.

Adding your own verifiable entropy, dice or an offline machine whose process you can audit, is what removes the single point of trust. I wrote up how to build that kind of air-gapped setup step by step: https://x.com/ForecastQuant/status/2123585216740528526

Most people never ask where their 24 words actually came from.
